title: File Transfer Protocol (FTP)

hero.subtitle: The classic file transfer protocol that pioneered client-server file sharing on the Internet, using separate control and data connections.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
FTP enables reliable file transfer between hosts on a TCP/IP network. It uses a unique dual-connection architecture: a persistent control connection for commands and a separate data connection for file transfers.

While largely replaced by SFTP and HTTPS for most use cases, FTP remains in use for legacy systems, firmware updates, and bulk file distribution.
sections.eli5: FTP is a way to copy files between two computers. It uses two phone lines: one stays open for talking about what you want, and a new one is opened each time a file actually has to be carried across.

sections.title: FTP Commands
sections.content:
USER/PASSAuthentication credentials
LISTList directory contents
RETRRetrieve (download) a file
STORStore (upload) a file
CWDChange working directory
PWDPrint working directory
PASVEnter passive mode
TYPESet transfer type (ASCII, Image, etc.)
QUITClose session
sections.eli5: You give the helper short written orders like "send me this file", "here is a file for you" or "go into that folder". Every order gets a numbered answer, so you always know whether it worked.

sections.title: Control and Data Connections
sections.content:
Control Connection
Data Connection
Port 21 (persistent)
Port 20 or dynamic (per-transfer)
Text commands/responses
File data / directory listings
Always TCP
Active or Passive mode

In active mode, the server connects back to the client for data transfer. In passive mode (PASV), the client initiates both connections. Passive mode is often needed for clients behind NAT or firewalls.
sections.eli5: The talking line and the carrying line are different. Normally the server rings you back for the carrying line, but if you have a locked front door that is a problem, so in passive mode you ring the server both times instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Original FTP transmits everything (including passwords) in cleartext, making it unsuitable for modern use without additional security layers.

FTPS (RFC 4217)
FTP over TLS - adds encryption, negotiated with the AUTH TLS command
SFTP
SSH File Transfer Protocol - a completely different protocol that runs over SSH (not FTP)
Modern Alternatives
HTTPS uploads, SCP, rsync over SSH, cloud storage APIs
sections.eli5: This old way of working sends your secret password written on a postcard that anyone along the way can read. Newer versions wrap the postcard in a locked box, and other tools do the same job with a lock built in.

references.text: Postel, J. and J. Reynolds, "File Transfer Protocol (FTP)", RFC 959, October 1985.
Ford-Hutchinson, P., "Securing FTP with TLS", RFC 4217, October 2005.

subtitle: The classic file transfer protocol, which uses one connection for commands and a separate one for each transfer.

tldr.problem: Hosts with different file systems and character sets need a common way to move files between them.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TCP control connection to port 21 and sends text commands such as USER, RETR and STOR. The server answers each with a three-digit reply code, and every file or listing travels over a separate data connection.
tldr.outcome: Its plain-text design sends passwords unencrypted and its two connections trouble firewalls and NAT, so FTP has mostly been replaced by HTTPS and SSH-based transfer.

eli5.summary: You talk to a helper on one phone line about what you want, and the helper sends the actual files over a second line. The first line stays open the whole time.

questions: what is the difference between active and passive ftp
why does ftp use two connections
today: Plain FTP is mostly gone from the public Internet because it sends passwords and data in cleartext, and major web browsers have removed their built-in FTP support. It lingers for legacy systems, device firmware and bulk file distribution. FTP over TLS (RFC 4217), SFTP (a different protocol over SSH) and HTTPS have taken over most of the work. Passive mode, defined by the PASV command in this RFC, is what almost every modern client uses to get through firewalls and NAT.

viz.caption: Downloading a file in passive mode

messages.label: 220 Service ready for new user
messages.note: The client has connected to the server's control port 21.

messages.label: USER Doe
messages.note: Then PASS sends the password in cleartext; the server answers 331, then 230 User logged in.

messages.label: PASV
messages.note: Ask the server to listen on a non-default data port.

messages.label: 227 Entering Passive Mode (h1,h2,h3,h4,p1,p2)
messages.note: Four numbers for the server's IP address and two for its port.

messages.label: RETR test.pl1
messages.note: The client opens the data connection to the address and port from the 227 reply.

messages.label: 150 File status okay; about to open data connection
226 Closing data connection
messages.note: Sent after the server closes the data connection.

viz.caption: Sample session adapted from section 7 of the RFC

data.title: A typical FTP session (control connection)
data.code:
S: 220 Service ready
C: USER Doe
S: 331 User name ok, need password
C: PASS mumble
S: 230 User logged in
C: RETR test.pl1
S: 150 File status okay; about to open data connection
S: 226 Closing data connection, file transfer successful
C: TYPE I
S: 200 Command OK
C: STOR >udd>cn>fd
S: 550 Access denied
C: QUIT
